observed_title: Semidefinite Relaxations for Semi-Infinite Polynomial Programming
version: arXiv:1306.1875v1; 23 PDF pages. The text front matter identifies the 2013 preprint; publication venue/version was not normalized here.

read_ranges.scope: Entire extracted text: abstract, model, polynomial/SOS and moment relaxations, finite and infinite-index algorithms, proofs, examples, Appendices A and B, references, and author matter. Original PDF pages 3, 7, 8, 13, 14, 15, and 17 were rendered to inspect the core equations and theorem statements.

topic_relevance.B02: direct: develops an exchange/constraint-generation algorithm for semi-infinite polynomial programs, with global finite-dimensional SDP subproblems; treats compact index sets and a homogenization extension for noncompact sets. It is a concrete polynomial/SOS method, not a general convex-SIP oracle method.

definitions.name: Semi-infinite polynomial program (SIPP)
definitions.statement: Minimize polynomial f(x) over a compact semialgebraic decision set X, subject to the polynomial inequality g(x,u)≥0 for every u in a (possibly noncompact) infinite semialgebraic index set U.

definitions.name: Archimedean quadratic module
definitions.statement: Q(F) is Archimedean if some ψ∈Q(F) has a nonnegative set {x:ψ(x)≥0} that is compact. This assumption implies K is compact; compactness of K alone does not imply the given module is Archimedean, though one may add a redundant bounding constraint.

definitions.name: Flat truncation certificate
definitions.statement: An optimal truncated moment sequence y* has a flat truncation if rank M_{t−d}(y*)=rank M_t(y*) for some t in the specified degree range. The cited result uses this condition to certify finite convergence and extract global minimizers.

definitions.name: Exchange subproblems
definitions.statement: At iteration k, keep a finite index set U_k, solve the restricted global optimization problem P_k, then globally minimize g(x_k,u) over U; if the minimum is negative, add global minimizers of that separation problem to the index set.

definitions.name: Homogenized index sets
definitions.statement: For polynomial constraints h_i(u)≥0, normalize the homogenized coordinates to the unit sphere and distinguish U_0 with u_0>0, its closure, and the compact relaxation eU with u_0≥0. Boundary points u_0=0 encode limiting directions and can add constraints.

definitions.name: Closed at infinity
definitions.statement: The paper calls the set closed at infinity when closure(U_0)=eU.

theorem_cards.label: Theorem 2.2 (Putinar certificate, cited result)
assumptions: The quadratic module Q(F) satisfies the stated Archimedean condition.
The polynomial p is strictly positive on the feasible set K.
theorem_cards.statement: Then p belongs to Q(F). This yields asymptotic convergence of the Lasserre hierarchy after applying the result to f−f*+ε; it does not itself assert finite convergence.
proof_steps: The authors cite Putinar’s Positivstellensatz; no proof is supplied in this paper.
Under strict positivity, apply the certificate to f−f*+ε for any ε>0, producing hierarchy values arbitrarily close to the global value when the Archimedean hypothesis holds.
gaps: This is cited background rather than a theorem proved in the paper. Strict positivity and Archimedean assumptions must be preserved; merely compact K does not imply the original module is Archimedean without a redundant bounding constraint.

theorem_cards.label: Proposition 3.3 (monotonicity of restricted problem values)
assumptions: Each restricted problem P_k has a global optimum.
The finite index sets are nested U_1⊆U_2⊆…⊆U.
theorem_cards.statement: The restricted minima satisfy f_1^min≤f_2^min≤…≤f*, where f* is the original SIPP optimum.
proof_steps: Adding index constraints shrinks the feasible sets, so the minimum cannot decrease.
The full feasible set is contained in every restricted feasible set, so each restricted minimum is no larger than f*.
gaps: The statement concerns exact global minima of the restricted problems; numerical SDP lower bounds are an additional relaxation layer.

theorem_cards.label: Theorem 3.4 (exchange convergence)
assumptions: At every iteration the restricted primal problems P_k and separation problems Q_k^i are solved globally.
The intermediate global minimizer sets S_k and at least one separation-minimizer set T_k^i are nonempty.
For the limit-point proof, U is compact and g is continuous so v(x)=min_{u∈U}g(x,u) is continuous.
theorem_cards.statement: The exchange algorithm either terminates finitely with a global solution of P, or every limit point of any sequence x_k∈S_k is a global solution of P. The implementation’s tolerance test g_k^i≥−ε gives an ε-feasibility certificate, not the theorem’s exact finite-stop conclusion.
proof_steps: Nested index sets yield nested feasible regions and monotone restricted optimal values bounded above by f*.
At exact finite stopping, the selected restricted minimizer satisfies every semi-infinite constraint; its restricted value and global feasibility force its objective to equal f*.
Otherwise, compactness of X gives subsequential limit points. Each previously generated constraint is eventually included, so every limit point satisfies it.

For a minimizing index u_k at x_k, the violated-cut value v(x_k)=g(x_k,u_k) is compared with g at the limit point; continuity (uniform over compact U) and feasibility of the limit point for the accumulated cuts give v(limit)≥0.
Feasibility plus the monotone restricted values implies the limit objective equals f*.
gaps: The theorem statement’s explicit assumptions list compactness of X and exact global solves/nonempty subproblem solutions; the proof also invokes compact U and continuity of v, which is established in the surrounding discussion but should be kept explicit when transferring it.
No iteration-complexity bound is proved. Numerical termination with ε>0 is approximate.

theorem_cards.label: Proposition 4.2 (homogenized nonnegativity equivalence)
assumptions: q is a polynomial on U defined by finitely many polynomial inequalities.
q~ and the defining inequalities are homogenized using their degrees; U_0 is normalized with u_0>0.
theorem_cards.statement: q(u)≥0 on U if and only if its homogenization q~ is nonnegative on closure(U_0).
proof_steps: If q is negative at some feasible v, the normalized point (1,v)/sqrt(1+||v||²) lies in U_0 and the homogenized value is a positive scaling of q(v), so nonnegativity fails.
Conversely, approximate any point in closure(U_0) by normalized points with u_0>0 arising from U; continuity of q~ passes nonnegativity to the limit.
gaps: This identifies closure(U_0), not automatically the larger compact set eU. Replacing closure(U_0) by eU can strengthen constraints unless U is closed at infinity.

theorem_cards.label: Theorem 4.6 (value comparison under homogenization)
assumptions: The compact-index relaxation uses eU; the original problem uses U.
If equality of values is claimed, U must be closed at infinity: closure(U_0)=eU.
theorem_cards.statement: The homogenized problem’s optimum is at least the original optimum; the values are equal when U is closed at infinity.
proof_steps: Proposition 4.2 identifies the original feasible set with constraints indexed by closure(U_0).
Since closure(U_0)⊆eU, the homogenized feasible set is contained in the original one, so its minimum is no smaller.
If U is closed at infinity, the index sets agree, hence so do feasible sets and values.
gaps: The source’s Example 4.8 shows equality can fail: eU may contain boundary directions not approximable from U_0 and can eliminate all otherwise feasible decisions.

theorem_cards.label: Theorem 4.10 (algebraic exceptional conditions for failure at infinity)
assumptions: U is defined by the polynomial inequalities in §4.
The proof uses the source’s Lemma 4.9 and resultant/discriminant propositions in Appendix B.
theorem_cards.statement: If U is not closed at infinity, the indicated leading-form resultants vanish when |J|>p, or the indicated discriminant vanishes when |J|≤p. The authors infer that closedness at infinity is generic for generic defining polynomials.
proof_steps: A missing boundary direction yields a common zero of the selected highest-degree homogeneous parts and the sphere equation.
Lemma 4.9 makes the corresponding Jacobian rank deficient in the small-|J| case; Appendix B propositions convert common zeros/rank deficiency into vanishing resultant/discriminant conditions.
Avoiding these algebraic degeneracies is the basis for the authors’ genericity claim.

proof_basis_ranges.scope: Appendix B definitions/propositions on resultants and discriminants cited by the theorem.

gaps: “Generic” is not assigned a precise topology/probability notion in the displayed conclusion; the theorem gives necessary algebraic degeneracy conditions for failure, not a practical closed-at-infinity test for a particular model. I read the complete cited appendix but did not independently establish the measure/algebraic-geometric genericity claim.

constant_dependence.explicit: No numerical error bound, iteration complexity, or dimension-dependent constant is established for the exchange sequence. The convergence claim is qualitative under exact global subproblem solves.
constant_dependence.dependence: The convergence argument depends on compactness of the decision domain X; separation minimizers must exist, and compact index sets plus continuity make the value function continuous. SDP hierarchy convergence further depends on Archimedean/positivity assumptions; flatness is a separate finite extraction certificate.

endpoint_limits.index_boundary: For noncompact U, homogenization adds boundary points with u_0=0. Those points represent directions at infinity and must be checked: closedness at infinity is the condition under which indexing by eU preserves feasibility/value.
endpoint_limits.exact_vs_tolerant: The theorem is exact, while Algorithm 3.1’s practical stop condition uses tolerance ε; a point whose minimum separation value is at least −ε is only ε-feasible.
endpoint_limits.relaxation_order: Lasserre’s hierarchy converges asymptotically under the stated Archimedean condition; finite convergence and minimizer extraction require flat truncation or the separate Jacobian SDP construction and its assumptions.
endpoint_limits.scope: The method specifically exploits polynomial/SOS structure and exact global optimization subroutines. It is not a generic guarantee for arbitrary convex SIP or inexact separation oracles.

reusable_methods.method: Finite exchange loop with a globally solved master problem and global separation subproblem; add all obtained worst-case minimizers, and certify stopping with the minimum constraint residual.
reusable_methods.transfer: For polynomial models, use moment/SOS or Jacobian SDP hierarchies for global solves. Preserve the exact assumptions behind global solves and nonempty minimizer sets; in approximate implementations, report ε-feasibility separately from exact global optimality.

reusable_methods.method: Homogenize a polynomial index set, normalize to a compact sphere, and represent noncompact-index constraints through closure(U_0).
reusable_methods.transfer: Before replacing closure(U_0) by eU, verify closedness at infinity or report the resulting conservative relaxation. The u_0=0 boundary is essential.

reusable_methods.method: Use flat truncation rank equality as a finite-convergence and optimizer-extraction check for moment/SOS relaxations.
reusable_methods.transfer: Do not infer finite convergence from compactness or a low hierarchy order alone; the flatness condition is checked on a feasible optimal moment sequence.

unchecked: All 23 PDF pages and appendices were read. Pages 3, 7, 8, 13, 14, 15, and 17 were rendered with PyMuPDF to visually inspect the SOS/algorithm/homogenization equations.

The reported numerical experiments were not rerun. I did not independently verify external cited results such as Putinar’s theorem or the algebraic genericity claim beyond checking the paper’s stated derivation and its included appendix.
The line extraction has visible layout/OCR noise (e.g. date/arXiv text and some stacked equations); theorem statements used here were checked against the rendered PDF pages.
